why.4: F-06 and Summary item 1 flag that the high-fire rule does not divert fumes. FR-RTO6-017 and the DIVERTING sequence open XV-602 and close XV-601 below divert low limit SP-601-03. They also remove the 'RTO-6 on-line' signal to CL-6 and request a CL-6 stop on failure.
why.5: F-06 notes that 'falls below' has no deadband or delay and adds a delay and hysteresis. why.6: F-09 and FR-RTO6-020 accept STOP from PURGING, HEATING, and HOT STANDBY, which then go to COOLING. The state table gives fan behavior: Run in COOLING, and 'Run if available' in TRIPPED. F-10 states that the fan runs during cool-down.

why.1: F-13 flags that FAULT has no exit. T-12 and T-13 define operator RESET with the cause cleared, plus TT-601 and K-601 conditions. They route to COOL-DOWN or OFF, and automatic burner restart is forbidden.
why.2: The output moves purge timing to the BMS, lists 'airflow proven' for K-601 in PURGE, and F-06 adds fan permissives. It never flags that the purge relies on a timer alone. It also never requires airflow to stay proven for the whole purge time, or the purge to restart if airflow is lost.
why.3: F-08 flags opening XV-601 from the faceplate as a device action, not a state command, with no permissives. It is replaced with an ADMIT FUMES command running SEQ-ADM with permissives (T-05), and the faceplates are locked in AUTO.
why.4: F-10 flags that 'high fire' leaves fumes admitted below destruction temperature. It adds an automatic PROCESS→READY divert at the low-temperature divert limit via SEQ-DIV. SEQ-DIV opens XV-602, closes XV-601, and clears 'fumes treated' to CL-6.
why.5: F-03 flags that the single 760 C value serves as both the READY permissive and the PROCESS control action with no deadband, so it chatters. It defines separate setpoints, a divert reset deadband, and a hold time.
why.6: T-09 defines STOP from PURGE to OFF, and T-08 defines STOP from HEAT-UP to COOL-DOWN. The states table puts K-601 running in COOL-DOWN, and in TRIPPED 'running for cool-down unless a fan fault'. T-10 keeps K-601 running on cool-down timeout.

why.1: Item 7 says FAULT is a dead end with no way back to OFF. The transitions table defines the exits: FAULT goes to COOL-DOWN when the trip cause is cleared, the operator resets, TT-601 ≥ T_cool and the fan is available. It goes to OFF when the cause is cleared, the operator resets and TT-601 < T_cool. It also states there is no direct path from FAULT to PURGE or any firing state.
why.2: Item 5 says a bare 5-minute timer proves nothing. It requires the combustion fan to be proven running with an airflow or DP switch and purge airflow at or above the minimum. why.3: Item 1 says opening XV-601 from the HMI faceplate is a raw command, not an interlocked transition. The operator should request PROCESS and the sequence opens XV-601 only when permissives are met. The READY to ADMITTING transition lists those permissives.
why.4: Item 3 says low temperature in PROCESS only triggers high fire and requires a low limit that diverts fumes and returns to HEAT-UP. The DIVERTING state opens XV-602 and closes XV-601, and sends a 'diverted' signal to CL-6. Item 15 covers the CL-6 signals.
why.5: Item 12 says there is no hysteresis or debounce on 760 °C and that one threshold used for both READY and PROCESS will chatter. The corrected model separates T_permit and T_low and adds time delays.
why.6: Stop from PURGE goes to OFF and Stop from HEAT-UP or READY goes to COOL-DOWN. Item 13 and the outputs table require the fan to run during COOL-DOWN, with loss of the fan handled. The trip table gives the fan action after each FAULT cause.

why.1: Item 7 flags 'There is no exit from FAULT.' The FAULT definition and transition table set the reset conditions as 'All trips clear and operator reset' and the state entered after reset as OFF, so any restart re-purges.
why.2: Item 5 flags that 'Purge is timer-only.' It requires the combustion fan running with airflow proven, and states the timer must reset if any purge condition is lost mid-purge. The PURGE state row repeats this.
why.3: Item 4 says opening XV-601 from the faceplate lets the state machine be bypassed. It requires XV-601 to be commanded only by sequence logic after permissives, with the operator requesting PROCESS. The READY to PROCESS transition lists those permissives.

why.6: Fan behavior is defined: on during COOL-DOWN, and on during FAULT unless the trip is fan-related. Stop/Shutdown is defined only from READY and PROCESS. No Stop transition is given from PURGE or HEAT-UP, so this part of the expectation is missing.

why.1: The hold table stops the feed when SI-501 is below minimum speed and when temperature exceeds the hold limit or the 88 °C alarm. There is no condition for loss of cooling margin, such as TV-506A or the cooling demand near full open or saturated. Only valve faults and the cascade leaving auto are covered.
why.2: Restarting re-checks permissives and repeats the initiation step after an agitation-loss hold before resuming full rate. It requires operator confirmation after an agitator or accumulation hold and ramps back from the current totalizer value, so restart is an explicit action with accumulation-limiting conditions.
why.3: Section 5 sets a heat-release indicator from the jacket heat balance and the reactor-to-jacket ΔT, and compares monomer fed with the amount the heat release says has reacted. It adds a low-cooling-demand backstop. In both cases the action is to hold the feed with FIC-510 closed.
why.4: Section 7 defines Holding/Held, Restarting, Stopping and Aborting. Each covers FIC-510 and feed valve positions, agitator status and temperature control: TIC-505/506 stay active, and on Abort TV-506B is held closed with cooling left available.
why.5: The totalizer reaching the recipe target is the completion condition. However, there is no rule for a feed that takes much longer than expected, such as a maximum feed time or elapsed-time deviation. Elapsed time is only reported.
why.6: Section 8 states the 95 °C SIS is independent and that the phase does not depend on, bypass or reset it. SIS feed isolation is done by the SIS itself, and the phase only reports the trip and goes to Abort.

why.1: The output stops the feed on SI-501 below minimum speed and on high reactor temperature (a feed-stop value below 88 C, and the 88 C alarm). It never covers loss of cooling margin, such as TV-506A or the cooling demand near full open or saturated. Its cooling-related checks only look for too little heat release or steam being called.
why.2: Loss of agitation sends the phase to Hold with 'Do not resume until agitation is restored and the accumulation check is satisfied.' Leaving Hold needs an ISA-88 Restart. Restart re-checks permissives, does not resume at full rate, and re-verifies consumption through the heat-release indicator or a small restart quantity, which limits accumulation.
why.3: Detection uses monomer fed against consumption estimated from reaction heat (cooling demand or jacket duty), the reactor-to-jacket temperature difference, falling temperature, and steam demand. The action is to stop the feed and go to Hold. An initiation check also stops the feed if onset is not confirmed.
why.4: Hold, Restart, Stop and Abort are each defined. They state the feed valve closed and FIC-510 at 0, the agitator state, TIC-505/506 kept in cascade (Hold and Stop), maximum cooling with steam TV-506B closed and locked out (Abort), and the conditions for resuming on Restart.
why.5: Completion uses the totalized delivered quantity against the recipe total. There is no rule for a feed that takes much longer than expected, such as a maximum feed-time alarm or timeout.
why.6: The SIS is stated to be independent; the phase does not bypass, reset, or depend on it. The phase only detects a trip and aborts its own outputs, and leaves any hardwired feed closure as an open item.

why.1: Start sequence (5.1, FR-CONV-008) is CV-3, CR-1, CV-2, CV-1, VF-1. Each conveyor is proven by its ZSL showing motion within SP-03 before the next start (FR-CONV-009/010). CR-1 is proven by lube pressure and current, and VF-1 by run feedback, which suits drives without zero-speed switches.
why.2: Normal stop (5.2, FR-CONV-020/021) runs VF-1, CV-1, CV-2, CR-1, CV-3. Each conveyor runs out for its own SP-05 time (20-45 s, set per conveyor) so belts are emptied.
why.3: Class 2 response stops the affected drive and all upstream drives at once, while downstream drives run out in flow order. It applies to misalignment trip, zero speed, plugged chute and CR-1 faults (6.2/6.3, FR-CONV-040).
why.4: The output says pull-cords act through the hardwired safety circuit, the PLC is not in the stop path, and the narrative only monitors status (FR-CONV-030/031). It never requires a local reset at the pull-cord before restart. The only reset described is RESET on the HMI.
why.5: CR-1 current high is alarm-only (Class 3) and high-high trips CR-1 and upstream. Nothing reduces or stops feed (VF-1) to head off an overload. The thresholds SP-20/SP-21 are TBD, not defined.
why.6: SP-01 sets a 10 s warning before any conveyor moves (FR-CONV-004/005). FR-CONV-044 requires any restart after a trip to use the full start sequence including the warning. All starts from Stopped go through step 2.

why.1: SQ-LINE-START starts CV-3, CR-1, CV-2, CV-1, VF-1 in that order (FR-LINE-020). Each step waits for proof before the next (FR-LINE-023). Conveyors are proven by their SSL zero-speed switches. CR-1 and VF-1 have no zero-speed switch, so they are proven by lube pressure/current and running feedback.
why.2: SQ-LINE-STOP stops VF-1 first, then CV-1, CV-2, CR-1, CV-3. Each stop waits for that unit's own run-out time (SP-LINE-005/006/007, CR-1 clear time SP-LINE-008), and FR-LINE-031 requires a separate run-out time per conveyor.
why.3: Section 6.1 trip response rule and table: the faulted unit and all upstream units stop at once, while downstream units run out and stop in flow order. FR-LINE-050 applies this to every trip.
why.4: Section 6.2 notes say the pull-cord stops the drive through the hardwired circuit and the BPCS only reads status and gives first-out indication. FR-LINE-070 requires a local pull-cord reset before HMI RESET is accepted.
why.5: CR-1 current is used only for a high-current alarm (no stop) and a high-high trip, and both thresholds are TBD. Reducing or stopping feed on high current is not specified; it is deferred to open item OI-05.
why.6: SP-LINE-001 sets 10 s, and FR-LINE-021 requires the warning before any conveyor run command. Every start, including after a stop or a trip (Tripped -> RESET -> Stopped -> START per T8/T1 and FR-LINE-104), goes through SQ-LINE-START step S1 warning, and the controller never restarts units by itself (FR-LINE-105).

why.1: Section 2 starts the line in the order CV-3, CR-1, CV-2, CV-1, VF-1. Each conveyor is proven by its zero-speed switch before the next device starts. CR-1 is proven by current and lube pressure, since it has no zero-speed switch. The start aborts if any device fails to prove.
why.2: Section 4.1 stops VF-1 first, then each device in flow order. Each conveyor has its own run-out timer (adj. 20-45 s, set from measured empty time), and the timers are explicitly individual per conveyor so belts are emptied.
why.3: Section 4.2 states that the tripped device and everything upstream stop immediately, while downstream devices run out on their normal timers. A per-device table supports this. Pull-cord is a stated safety exception.
why.4: The output does require a local reset at the cord. However, it only says the function 'should be hardwired or SIL-rated and independent of the PLC, which this narrative does not cover', and otherwise treats pull-cords as PLC trips. It never states that pull-cords act directly on the motor circuit with the PLC only monitoring them.
why.5: The CR-1 current table defines a high-current alarm at 105% FLA (about 220 A) that reduces VF-1 to minimum speed, before the overload trip at 120% FLA (about 250 A), with delays defined.
why.6: The 10 s horn and beacon warning runs before the first conveyor moves. Section 4.3 states that any restart after a trip is a full Line Start including the 10 s warning, and every start goes through the same sequence.

why.1: Section 4.2 starts in the order CV-3, CR-1, CV-2, CV-1, VF-1. Each step waits until the previous one is proven running. Conveyors are proven by ZSS motion within 10 s. CR-1 has no ZSS, so it is proven by lube pressure and run-up current instead.
why.2: Section 5 stops VF-1 first, then each machine in flow order. Each step has its own run-out timer, set per conveyor from the 20-45 s range, measured at commissioning with about 10% margin, so belts and the crusher are emptied.
why.3: Principle 2 and Sections 6.1 and 6.4 stop the faulted device and everything upstream immediately. Downstream equipment runs out on the normal stop timers, with a table for each fault origin.
why.4: Pull-cords are hardwired into the motor starter control circuits, independent of the PLC, and the PLC monitors them for indication and restart logic. A trip stays latched until the cord is reset locally, then the reset is acknowledged at the HMI.
why.5: Section 6.2 sets an alarm at 105% FLC (220 A). Feed cutback at 110% FLC (231 A) stops VF-1 until current falls below 100%, before the trip at 120% FLC (252 A).
why.6: Section 4.1 runs a 10 s horn and beacon before any movement. The warning repeats in full on every start or restart, including after a trip, and Section 7 restates it for restarts.

why.1: R-10 flags the 'any circuit' start as a product-safety risk with no proof that S-1/HTST-1 is out of production and no mix-proof valve position feedback. FR-CIP-003 requires the circuit to be out of production and the mix-proof valves to be in the CIP lineup before start.
why.2: FR-CIP-004 and Steps 2/4 gate the timer on TT-501 and FT-501 only. Return conductivity is not a timer condition, and the output only says the timer starts when values are in range. It does not say the timer pauses or extends when they drop mid-step.
why.3: 'Heated to temperature' becomes heat to SP-04 with TT-501 at or above SP-05. 'Run until clean' becomes CT-501 at or below SP-16 held for SP-17, with a timeout. Values are TBD, but the criteria are defined against named setpoints.
why.4: P-502 failure is covered: FR-CIP-006 stops P-501, goes to Holding, and alarms. Low supply flow on FT-501 has no defined automatic response. FT-501 only appears as a timer-start condition and in bad-quality handling.
why.5: R-05 and FR-CIP-005 mention using CT-501 for the rinse/chemical cut. No recovery-to-tank versus drain logic based on return conductivity is defined. It is deferred to OI-05, and the chemical steps do not specify return routing.

why.1: R-04 names the risk of chemical reaching S-1 or HTST-1 while product is in service. FR-CIP-002 requires, before start, that the selected circuit is out of production, the mix-proof valves isolate the other circuit, and the other circuit is not in CIP.
why.2: R-08, Step 2/4 and FR-CIP-008 say the wash timer runs only while TT-501, CT-501 and FT-501 are in range. The FAT test checks that the timer does not run when TT-501 is below the limit, so the timer pauses on low temperature or conductivity.
why.3: 'Run until clean' becomes 'CT-501 at or below the final-rinse setpoint for the hold time' plus a timeout. 'Heated to temperature' becomes a TT-501 in-range timer condition against per-circuit setpoints. These are set values in the setpoint list rather than literal numbers, which the expectation's 'set value' wording allows.
why.4: FR-CIP-006 states that when P-502 stops, the system stops P-501, goes to Hold, alarms and prompts the operator. FR-CIP-005 puts the sequence in Hold with an alarm on low FT-501 flow, and Held means pumps are stopped. This replaces 'operator should check'.
why.5: Each step has a fixed return route (drain or tank). There is no conductivity-based changeover between recovery to tank and drain at step transitions; chemical recovery and drain changeover are deferred to open item OI-02.

why.1: The output calls unrestricted circuit selection the most serious gap and notes S-1 and HTST-1 are product-contact equipment. Its start permissives require the circuit to be out of production, empty and flagged product-free, route valves confirmed by feedback, and other circuits isolated by mix-proof valves with no leak-chamber alarm.
why.2: The caustic and acid holds start only when TT-501 ≥ setpoint and CT-501 is within band. All timers run only while step conditions are satisfied. The timer pauses if TT-501 drops below setpoint during the hold.
why.3: 'Heated to temperature' becomes TT-501 ≥ [x] °C, and 'until clean' becomes CT-501 ≤ [x µS/cm] stable for [x] s with a minimum time. Both are instrument-based setpoint criteria, with values left as placeholders to be confirmed.
why.4: Fault handling is automatic. If P-502 stops, P-501 stops immediately, the sequence goes to HOLD, an alarm is raised and the timer freezes, with abort after a timeout. FT-501 low flow raises an alarm and HOLD, then aborts. P-501 is interlocked to run only while P-502 runs.
why.5: The output states that chemical-to-rinse transitions use CT-501 to divert the return stream to chemical recovery or drain. Caustic returns to its tank and rinses go to drain.

why.1: Problem 5 calls 'any circuit selected' unsafe because nothing checks that the circuit is out of production or that the mix-proof valves are proven. Section 7.2.1 requires the circuit to be not in production and empty (S-1) or in cleaning mode (HTST-1), mix-proof valves proven in CIP position by feedback, the other circuit isolated, and no leak-detection alarm before start. The product-contamination risk is implied rather than stated outright, but the required proofs are explicit.
why.2: The timer starts on TT-501 ≥ T_min and FT-501 ≥ flow SP, and pauses on low flow or low temperature. Return conductivity is only an end condition and an alarm. A conductivity drop does not pause or extend the wash timer, so the conductivity half of the expectation is missing.
why.3: 'Heated to temperature' becomes a defined caustic setpoint [T_caustic] with a TT-501 minimum. 'Until clean' becomes CT-501 ≤ [x] µS/cm (within [y] of rinse supply) for [z] s, with minimum and maximum times. These are measurable set-value criteria, with numbers left as placeholders for validation.
why.4: Section 7.2.4 handles a P-502 stop automatically: stop P-501 immediately, raise a high-priority alarm, put the sequence in HOLD. Section 7.2.3 handles low FT-501 flow automatically: alarm after a delay and pause the timer. Neither is left to the operator.
why.5: The output states that caustic and acid return to their tanks, that water/chemical changeover uses CT-501 thresholds, and that the mixed phase is diverted to drain. Step 3 displaces caustic to its tank and sends rinse to drain.
